newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban foes push south towards Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Taleban foes push south towards Kabul.

text.p: The forces of ousted Afghan government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood made major gains in overnight fighting north of Kabul, witnesses said on Saturday.

Backed by the artillery of northern Uzbek chief Abdul Rashid Dostum, Masood thrust towards Kabul in two directions, taking the Bagram airbase 60 km (40 miles) from the capital and the market town of Qarabagh on the road south.
Reporters who visited the two areas found Masood's jubilant men in firm control with more reinforcements arriving.
"Now we're ready to push them (the Taleban) out of Kabul," said beaming Masood commander Karim Mohab Rahman in Qarabagh.
"We captured Qarabagh last night at about two o'clock in the morning. We came with three tanks and 600 men and the Taleban withdrew without a fight," Rahman said.
Tanks swarming with Masood's ethnic Tajik soldiers churned south to Qarabagh, a 45-minute drive north of Kabul, accompanied by truck-mounted anti-aircraft and multiple-rocket launchers.
The Taleban, who swept into Kabul on September 27, appeared to be setting up new defensive positions about 10 km (six miles) south of Qarabagh.
They also appeared to be setting up similiar positions about the same distance south of Bagram on a parallel road leading to Kabul, but heavy shelling made it difficult to pinpoint their positions.
Taleban spokesmen in Kabul were not available for comment on Saturday and reporters were prevented from travelling north on the main road, which was closed to civilian traffic.
A Taleban officer at a roadblock just outside the city said several hundred Taleban fighters, along with tanks and multiple rocket launchers, had moved north along the main road early in the morning.

Blocking the road so near the city is usually a sign of a Taleban retreat, but the officer refused to admit they had suffered any setback, speaking of a counter-offensive that was pushing Masood back.

On the parallel road to Bagram, reporters were halted about 20 km (12 miles) south of the airbase, but the Taleban were preparing defensive positions farther back towards Kabul than those they occupied on Friday.

The loss of Bagram will be a major psychological blow to the ultra-conservative Taleban, even though they have been sending their small air force to attack Masood's positions from Kabul airport, not the airbase during days of fighting over it.

Hundreds of Masood's heavily armed men strolled around the now dilapidated airbase, once an ant hill of activity in the 1980s when the Soviet military threw its weight behind a communist government in Kabul.

Eight apparently useless fighter planes, several transport aircraft and helicopter carcasses of that era were parked in the base, but Masood's men said the Taleban had mined the area around them and it was not possible to inspect them.
Masood's men were also in control of the town of Bagram that bore few signs of the battle over it.
It was not immediately clear whether Masood intended to keep on driving south to Kabul, which he has twice demanded the Taleban leave, or give negotiators time to make a deal.
Several days of talks between the Taleban and Dostum this week have raised hopes that Kabul, extensively damaged in four years of factional fighting, would be spared another battle.

There has been no firm word of any outcome, but Pakistani newspapers said on Saturday President Farooq Leghari was scheduled to meet Dostum and Taleban leader Mullah Mohammad Omar in Uzbekistan's capital, Tashkent, on Saturday.
It would be the first time Omar, to whom it appears all major decisions are referred, has been directly involved in the talks.
